processing: Short wither, then pan-firing or steaming to stop oxidation, rolling and drying; some factories make needle-shaped or ball-rolled greens for export.
harvest_season: Spring (March–April) is the main green-tea season; some autumn lots.
appearance_dry: Twisted or needle-shaped dark green leaf, often with silver tips.
taste_profile: Fresh, sweet and lightly floral with mild vegetal notes and a clean, soft finish; gentler than most Chinese greens.

brewing.notes: Cool water, short steeps, no milk.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring lot from named factories and cooperatives; drink within the year, kept sealed and dark. Much of it is exported in bulk, so look for a seller who names the producer. No aged or vintage market.
description:
Nepal green tea comes from the same eastern hill districts as the country's orthodox black teas, Ilam, Dhankuta and Panchthar, and from the same Chinary and clonal bushes; the difference is that the leaf is fired before it can oxidise. Most factories make it in spring as a side line, and a few have made it a speciality, with needle-shaped and rolled styles aimed at export.

After a short wither the leaf is pan-fired or steamed, rolled and dried. Spring leaf gives the sweetest, most floral greens; later pickings are coarser and mostly go into bulk and tea bags.

The cup is pale yellow-green, fresh and sweet with a light floral note, mild vegetal character and a clean, soft finish; it is gentler than most Chinese greens and nothing like the umami-heavy Japanese style. Brew it at around 80 °C for two to three minutes, and keep the second steep short.

It is sold as the current year's spring lot from named factories and cooperatives, and much of it is exported in bulk, so look for a seller who names the producer. Drink it within the year, kept sealed and dark; there is no aged market.

If you enjoy Darjeeling green tea, this is the same idea at a better price, and often with a little more sweetness.
history:
Green tea is a side line of Nepal's orthodox industry, and its own history is thinly documented. The wider story is clearer: a first plantation in Ilam around 1863 and five eastern tea zones declared in 1982, among them Ilam, Panchthar and Dhankuta.

The move from subsistence crops to orthodox tea has been led by hillside smallholders, who grew 70 per cent of the country's orthodox tea in 2006. Green tea comes from the same gardens and farmers, with Ilam the centre of production.
